one_line_contribution: A generalizability-theory audit of agent-memory curation: randomize which bank items are injected, decompose realized episode-level item value into a stable item main effect vs item-by-query interaction vs decoding noise, derive the probe budget a reliable per-item ranking would require, and test on held-out instances whether pruning 'identified harmful' items beats removing the same number at random.
closest_prior_work: Two, and the proposal underweights one of them. (a) 'Helpful or Harmful Data? Fine-tuning-free Shapley Attribution' (arXiv:2406.04606) is the closest methodological threat, not merely a spiritual cousin: it already establishes the template that per-instance value scores are not sign-stable under resampling, which is the same negative-reliability story. The proposal's delta is a domain transplant (fine-tuning data -> injected memory items) plus off-the-shelf G-theory machinery and a random-removal transfer control. That is a real delta, but it is an increment on an existing critique rather than a new kind of claim, and the novelty score reflects that. (b) MEMAUDIT (arXiv:2605.02199) already asserts that memory value is set-level rather than per-item and builds an evaluation protocol on it; the proposal's honest position -- 'we supply the number MEMAUDIT presupposes' -- is exactly the position a reviewer reads as 'measures the constant in someone else's already-published qualitative claim'. Datamodels (Ilyas et al. 2022) supplies the estimator wholesale, so no methodological novelty is claimed there. Nothing here is scooped outright, but the conceptual headline is pre-owned and the statistics are borrowed; what remains genuinely unclaimed is the probe-budget derivation and the cross-proxy validity sweep in Phase 4.
strongest_objection: Two-part, and the first is not fixable with more compute. (1) PREMISE MISMATCH. The paper's target -- 'every curation method presumes an individual item has a stable estimable utility' -- is not what A-MAC, SAGE, EDV, AutoManual or Memory-R1 actually assert. They assert that a heuristic write/admit policy improves aggregate end-to-end performance. That claim survives intact even if per-item utility ranking is completely unreliable, exactly the way a noisy-but-biased filter can raise average quality without ranking any individual instance correctly. So P-2's headline comparison -- 'the generalizability formula implies >800 observations per item, one to two orders of magnitude above what A-MAC/SAGE/Memory-R1 spend per item' -- is a category error: those systems never claimed to rank items by realized downstream utility, and holding them to a ranking-reliability standard they never asserted is the kind of framing an AC calls a strawman. P5 and P6 partially rescue this by testing the published signals operationally, but note that P5 repurposes an admission score, calibrated on a write-time stream with its own base rates, as a deletion ranking inside an already-deduped 120-item bank; calling that 'faithful' will be contested. (2) THE NULL IS CONFOUNDED WITH A LOW CEILING. Every primary prediction (P-1, P-3, P-4, P-6) is a predicted null, and their informativeness depends entirely on the bank having item-level effects large enough that unreliability, rather than absence of signal, explains the result. The precheck only demands >=8% instance-level DISAGREEMENT vs no-memory in either direction -- directionless churn, which the track's own prior results say this setup produces in abundance. Removing 12 of 120 items from a bank whose total net contribution may be a point or two cannot plausibly move accuracy more than a fraction of the design's own ~3.8-point MDE, so P-4 landing inside its +/-4 band is close to arithmetically guaranteed regardless of whether item value is stable. P3 is offered as the ceiling, but P3 is estimated under the same randomized-injection distribution (k~U{1..6} over top-20) that Risk Factor 3 concedes differs from top-k deployment, so a null P3 is equally consistent with 'the estimand we measured is not the estimand deployment needs.' Relatedly, P-3 -- billed as 'the sharpest single number in the paper' -- is a restatement of the sample size: the proposal itself states the per-item detectable effect at ~85 binary observations is ~+/-20 points, so almost no item can clear a 95% CI bar. Pre-registering that your own per-item analysis is underpowered is not a finding about memory. (3) IDENTIFICATION. The hierarchical model has random effects for item, query, item x query and seed, but no term for item x co-injected-set. Items are injected in subsets of 1-6, so interference between co-injected items (the very combinatorial structure MEMAUDIT posits) has nowhere to go but the item x query term and the residual -- which means P-1's headline, 'item x query interaction is the largest component and the stable main effect is under 20%', can be produced by item-item interference that is nothing to do with query dependence. Worse, because probe items only appear on queries where the retriever ranks them top-20, most item x query cells have exactly one observation, so item x query and residual are confounded in the classic G-theory way; the 600-episode second-seed replicate identifies pure decoding noise but not the item x query vs item x set split.
what_would_fix_it: (a) Restate the audited premise as what the literature actually claims -- 'these signals improve end-to-end performance' -- and let P5/P6 vs P2 carry the indictment, rather than the probe-budget comparison, which should be demoted to a remark about what a per-item ranking would cost. (b) Add an ORACLE prune fit on the held-out episodes themselves (item effects estimated in-sample on the 800 test instances, then applied to those same instances). This is the only condition that separates 'per-item value is unstable' from 'there is nothing in this bank to find' and from 'the probe injection distribution is the wrong estimand'; without it a null P1/P3 is uninterpretable. (c) Run an explicit no-memory arm on the same 800 held-out instances (800 episodes, cheap) and report every delta as a fraction of the full-bank-minus-no-memory effect. If that denominator is ~2 points, say so up front; the paper is then a scoped null about a bank with little to curate, and should be written as such. (d) Strengthen the precheck from directionless churn to a signed requirement (full bank must beat or trail no-memory by an amount exceeding the null-replicate band) -- churn is exactly what the track's prior work already reports. (e) Add a pairwise (second-order) presence term or a datamodel interaction term so that item x co-injected-set variance is estimated rather than absorbed into item x query, and report the variance decomposition with and without it; P-1 as currently stated is not identified. (f) Make the variance-component ratio, not the CI-count P-3, the headline number.
missing_baseline: The query-conditional gate. The proposal's own finding -- value lives in item x query, not in the item -- immediately implies the constructive alternative is context-conditional filtering: learn or score item-query harm at retrieval time and gate per query, which is precisely Open Question 3 of the track brief ('given a memory item and a query, can harm be predicted before injection?'). The plan has no such arm. Every prune condition (P1, P3, P4, P5, P6) and the recommendation (P9, tune k globally) are query-agnostic, so the constructive corollary 'controlling the bank-level injection budget dominates item-level curation' is established only against the strictly weaker family the paper has just declared misconceived. A reviewer will say the study measures that item main effects are small and then tests only interventions that use item main effects. Two further omissions: (i) no no-memory arm on the 800-instance held-out set, so no delta has a denominator; (ii) no oracle/in-sample-on-test prune to upper-bound what any item-level curation could achieve on the actual test distribution. Separately, P9 is described as 'tune k on a dev split' without stating whether k=0 is in the search space -- if it is and it wins, the paper's finding is about this bank, not about curation.
preprint_collision: Above average for this kind of submission and unusually self-aware -- it names the single scenario that would gut the headline (a random-removal control appearing as an appendix ablation in a recent curation preprint) and reports that none of the nine retrieved papers contains one. Credit for that. But it is explicitly a single-pass, 14-query search whose second round was blocked, and the gap it admits is the one that matters most: 'generalizability theory applied to LLM evaluation' went unsearched, and that is exactly the query most likely to surface a collision, since variance-components and G-coefficient analyses of LLM-judge and agent-eval reliability are an active 2026 preprint area. Also unsearched, and relevant: datamodel/context-attribution work applied to retrieved context in RAG, and per-demonstration attribution under resampling beyond the one Shapley paper cited. No OpenReview 2026 sweep. I cannot name a preprint that already makes this exact claim, and the proposal's dispositions of MEMAUDIT (arXiv:2605.02199) and GovMem (arXiv:2607.02579) are argued rather than asserted, which is the right standard. But 'the search I did not run is the one aimed at my own method' is a real weakness, not a neutral, and the MEMAUDIT relationship -- conceding that MEMAUDIT already assumes package-level value and positioning this work as supplying its missing constant -- compresses the novelty claim more than the proposal admits.
